'''Scott Jay Kenyon''' (born 1956) is an American astrophysicist. His work has included advances in symbiotic and other types of interacting binary stars, the formation and evolution of stars, and the formation of planetary systems.

==Career==
Kenyon received a B.S. in physics from [[Arizona State University]] in 1978 and a Ph.D. in [[astronomy]] from the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]] in 1983. His doctoral dissertation is titled ''The Physical Structure of the Symbiotic Stars''<ref name="SS thesis">{{cite journal|title=Physical Nature of the Symbiotic Stars|publisher=NASA Astrophysics Data System|bibcode=1983PhDT.........8K|last1=Kenyon|first1=S. J.|date=1983|page=8}}</ref> and was expanded into a book, ''The Symbiotic Stars''.<ref name="SS book">{{cite book|title=The Symbiotic Stars|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|doi=10.1017/CBO9780511586071|year=1986|last1=Kenyon|first1=S. J.|isbn=9780511586071}}</ref>  After postdoctoral work at the [[Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics|Center for Astrophysics {{!}} Harvard & Smithsonian]], including a CfA Fellowship, he joined the scientific staff at the [[Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory]].{{citation needed|date=November 2012}}

Kenyon is a [[Fellow of the AAAS]], a Fellow<ref>{{cite web|title=2013 APS Fellows|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2013&unit_id=&institution=|accessdate=9 February 2014}}</ref> of the [[American Physical Society]], and is included in the [[Web of Knowledge]] index of highly cited researchers.<ref>{{cite web|title=Index of Highly Cited Researchers|url=http://highlycited.com/names/k/|publisher=Web of Knowledge|accessdate=25 October 2012}}</ref>

==Scientific work==
Kenyon has worked extensively on [[symbiotic binary]] stars.<ref name="SS">{{cite web|title=S. Kenyon publications on symbiotic stars|url=http://adsabs.harvard.edu/cgi-bin/nph-abs_connect?db_key=AST&db_key=PRE&qform=AST&arxiv_sel=astro-ph&arxiv_sel=cond-mat&arxiv_sel=cs&arxiv_sel=gr-qc&arxiv_sel=hep-ex&arxiv_sel=hep-lat&arxiv_sel=hep-ph&arxiv_sel=hep-th&arxiv_sel=math&arxiv_sel=math-ph&arxiv_sel=nlin&arxiv_sel=nucl-ex&arxiv_sel=nucl-th&arxiv_sel=physics&arxiv_sel=quant-ph&arxiv_sel=q-bio&sim_query=YES&ned_query=YES&adsobj_query=YES&aut_req=YES&aut_logic=AND&obj_logic=OR&author=kenyon%2C+s&object=&start_mon=&start_year=&end_mon=&end_year=&ttl_req=YES&ttl_logic=OR&title=%2Bsymbiotic%0D%0A%2Bnova&txt_logic=OR&text=&nr_to_return=200&start_nr=1&jou_pick=ALL&ref_stems=&data_and=ALL&group_and=ALL&start_entry_day=&start_entry_mon=&start_entry_year=&end_entry_day=&end_entry_mon=&end_entry_year=&min_score=&sort=CITATIONS&data_type=SHORT&aut_syn=YES&ttl_syn=YES&txt_syn=YES&aut_wt=1.0&obj_wt=1.0&ttl_wt=0.3&txt_wt=3.0&aut_wgt=YES&obj_wgt=YES&ttl_wgt=YES&txt_wgt=YES&ttl_sco=YES&txt_sco=YES&version=1}}</ref> His book ''The Symbiotic Stars'' was the first to summarize observations and theories for these interacting binaries.<ref name="Selvelli">{{cite journal |title=Book Review: The symbiotic stars |first=P. L. |last=Selvelli|journal=Space Science Reviews |volume=47 |issue = 3–4|page=402 |date=1988 |bibcode=1988SSRv...47..402S|doi=10.1007/BF00243559|s2cid=189788657 }}</ref> The book reviews the general state of knowledge in this field c. 1984 and contains case histories of well-studied binaries<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/full/seri/Obs../0107//0000170.000.html |title=Book Review: The symbiotic stars |first=D. |last=Stickland |journal=The Observatory |volume=107 |page=170 |date=August 1987 |bibcode=1987Obs...107..170S}}</ref> and complete references to all papers published on symbiotic stars before c. 1984.<ref>{{cite journal| title=Book review: The symbiotic stars| first=D. |last=Chochol |journal=Bulletin of the Astronomical Institutes of Czechoslovakia |volume=39 |issue = 2| page=128 |bibcode=1988BAICz..39..128C| year=1988 }}</ref> With more than 350 citations,<ref name="SS"/> the book is a standard in the field.

Kenyon and Lee Hartmann first worked out detailed [[accretion disk]] models for  [[pre–main sequence star]]s and applied these models to optical and infrared spectra of [[FU Orionis]] objects.<ref name="B89">{{cite journal | title=T Tauri Stars-Wild as Dust| first=C. | last=Bertout | journal=Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics |volume=27| page=351|bibcode=1989ARA&A..27..351B|doi = 10.1146/annurev.aa.27.090189.002031 | year=1989 }}</ref>
Aside from explaining many details in the spectra of [[FUors]],<ref name="B89" /><ref name="R90">{{citation | title=FU Orionis eruptions and early stellar evolution|journal=Flare Stars in Star Clusters |volume=137 |pages=229 |first=B. |last=Reipurth|bibcode=1990IAUS..137..229R|year=1990 }}</ref> observations of the size of the disk in FU Orionis match model predictions.<ref>{{cite journal|title=FU Orionis Resolved by Infrared Long-Baseline Interferometry at a 2 AU Scale| first=F.| last=Malbet|display-authors=etal | journal=Astrophysical Journal|volume=507| issue=2|page=L149| bibcode=1998ApJ...507L.149M|arxiv = astro-ph/9808326 |doi = 10.1086/311688 | year=1998| s2cid=14528716}}</ref> Observations of long-term variability in FUors also generally match model predictions.<ref name="C05">{{cite journal| title=The photometric evolution of FU Orionis objects: disc instability and wind-envelope interaction| first=C. |last=Clarke|author2=G. Lodato |author3=S. Y. Melnikov |author4=M. A. Ibrahimov | journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society| volume=361| issue=3 | pages=942–954 |bibcode=2005MNRAS.361..942C|arxiv = astro-ph/0505515 |doi = 10.1111/j.1365-2966.2005.09231.x | year=2005 | doi-access=free | s2cid=15471280 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Using FU Orionis outbursts to constrain self-regulated protostellar disk models|first=K. R.|last=Bell|author2=D. N. C. Lin |journal=Astrophysical Journal|volume=427|page=987|url=http://adsabs.harvard.edu.ezp-prod1.hul.harvard.edu/abs/1994ApJ...427..987B|bibcode=1994ApJ...427..987B|arxiv = astro-ph/9312015 |doi = 10.1086/174206 |year=1994|s2cid=118898339}}</ref> Kenyon and Hartmann used photometric observations and disk models to show that the disks of FUors are surrounded by infalling envelopes with a bipolar cavity.<ref name="C05" /> The bipolar cavity is a result of a wind<ref>{{cite journal|title=FU Orionis star winds|first=U.|last=Bastian|author2=R. Mundt |journal=Astronomy and Astrophysics|volume=144|page=57|bibcode=1985A&A...144...57B|year=1985}}</ref> from the disk, which interacts with the surrounding material to produce a [[bipolar outflow]] and (perhaps) a [[Herbig–Haro object]],.<ref name="R90" /><ref>{{cite journal|title=Herbig-Haro objects and FU Orionis eruptions The case of HH 57| first=B.| last=Reipurth| journal=Astronomy and Astrophysics| volume=143| page=435|bibcode=1985A&A...143..435R| year=1985}}</ref>

Kenyon and Hartmann later developed the first flared accretion disk model to explain the large infrared luminosities of [[T Tauri stars]].<ref name="CG97">{{cite journal|url=http://adsabs.harvard.edu.ezp-prod1.hul.harvard.edu/abs/1997ApJ...490..368C|title=Spectral Energy Distributions of T Tauri Stars with Passive Circumstellar Disks|first1=E. I.|last1=Chiang|author2=P. Goldreich |journal=Astrophysical Journal|volume=490|issue=1|pages=368–376|bibcode=1997ApJ...490..368C|arxiv = astro-ph/9706042 |doi = 10.1086/304869 |year=1997|s2cid=5938719}}</ref>
In this model, each concentric annulus of the disk is in [[hydrostatic equilibrium]]. The surface of the disk then flares upward like the surface of a shallow bowl.  A flared disk intercepts and re-radiates more light from the central star than a flat disk, producing a larger predicted infrared luminosity which agrees with observations of T Tauri stars.<ref name="CG97" /> Theoretical images<ref>{{cite journal|title=Model scattering envelopes of young stellar objects. I - Method and application to circumstellar disks|first=Barbara A.|last=Whitney|author2=Lee Hartmann |journal=Astrophysical Journal| volume=395| page=529| bibcode=1992ApJ...395..529W|doi = 10.1086/171673 |year=1992}}</ref> of edge-on flared disks look identical to actual images,<ref>{{cite journal|title=Hubble Space Telescope Observations of the Disk and Jet of HH 30|first=Christopher J. |last=Burrows|display-authors=etal |journal=Astrophysical Journal|volume=473|page=437|bibcode=1996ApJ...473..437B|doi=10.1086/178156|url=http://authors.library.caltech.edu/53760/1/34479.pdf|year=1996 |s2cid=51756708 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=An Edge-On Circumstellar Disk in the Young Binary System HK Tauri|first=Karl R. |last=Stapelfeldt |journal=Astrophysical Journal |volume=502|issue=1 | page=L65|bibcode=1998ApJ...502L..65S|doi = 10.1086/311479 |year=1998 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=HUBBLE SPACE TELESCOPE/NICMOS Imaging of Disks and Envelopes around Very Young Stars|first=Deborah L.|last=Padgett|display-authors=etal |journal=Astronomical Journal |volume=117|issue=3|pages=1490–1504|bibcode=  1999AJ....117.1490P|doi=10.1086/300781|arxiv = astro-ph/9902101 |year=1999|s2cid=16498360}}</ref> taken with the [[Hubble Space Telescope]], illustrating direct evidence for flared disks.<ref>{{cite journal|title=High-Resolution Near-Infrared Images and Models of the Circumstellar Disk in HH 30|first=Angela |last=Cotera|display-authors=etal |journal=Astrophysical Journal|volume=556|issue=2 |page=958|bibcode=2001ApJ...556..958C|doi=10.1086/321627|arxiv=astro-ph/0104066|year=2001 |s2cid=14354548 }}</ref>

In 1990, Kenyon, Hartmann, [[Karen Strom]] & Steve Strom identified the luminosity problem: [[protostars]] in the [[Taurus Molecular Cloud|Taurus-Auriga star-forming region]] are approximately 10 times less luminous than predicted by star formation theory.<ref name="MO2011">{{citation|title=The Luminosity Problem: Testing Theories of Star Formation |first1=C. F.|last1=McKee |last2=Offner|first2=S.R.R. |bibcode=2011IAUS..270...73M|arxiv = 1010.4307 |doi = 10.1017/S1743921311000202 |volume=6 |journal=Proceedings of the International Astronomical Union |pages=73–80|year=2010|s2cid=118314634}}</ref> In this theory, protostars form by [[gravitational collapse]] of a cloud of gas and dust. Over their lifetimes, protostars radiate a total energy comparable to their binding energy. With apparent lifetimes of about 100,000 yr, they have expected luminosities of 10-20 larger than the [[solar luminosity]].  Recent observations of larger numbers of protostars with the [[Spitzer Space Telescope]] confirm that protostars have typical luminosities closer to the solar luminosity.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Evolutionary Signatures in the Formation of Low-Mass Protostars. II. Toward Reconciling Models and Observations|first=M.M.|last=Dunham| journal=Astrophysical Journal|volume=710|issue=1|pages=470–502|bibcode=2010ApJ...710..470D|arxiv = 0912.5229 |doi = 10.1088/0004-637X/710/1/470 |year=2010|s2cid=14156633}}</ref> Kenyon and colleagues identified several possible solutions to this luminosity problem. Adopting larger ages allows protostars to radiate the same amount of energy over a longer time, reducing their average luminosity. If [[protostars]] spend a small fraction of their lifetimes at much higher luminosity, as in the [[FU Orionis stars]], then their average luminosity can be much larger than their typical luminosity. McKee & Offner note that ejecting material in a bipolar outflow reduces the expected luminosity of protostars but does not resolve the luminosity problem.<ref name="MO2011" /> Data from [[Spitzer]] resolve the luminosity problem by deriving better estimates for the time spent in a high luminosity state and larger ages of 300,000 yr for protostars.<ref name="PLF">{{cite journal| title=The Protostellar Luminosity Function|author=Offner, S. S. R.|author2=McKee, C. F. |journal=Astrophysical Journal|volume=736|issue=1|page=53|bibcode=2011ApJ...736...53O|arxiv = 1105.0671 |doi = 10.1088/0004-637X/736/1/53 |year=2011|s2cid=118784638}}</ref> This resolution leads to an improved understanding of the early life histories of stars.<ref name="MO2011" /><ref name="PLF" />

Kenyon has developed numerical models for planet formation and applied these calculations to the formation of [[debris disks]]<ref>{{cite journal|title=Are debris disks self-stirred?|first=G.M. |last=Kennedy|author2=M.C. Wyatt |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society| volume=405|issue=2 |page=1253|bibcode=2010MNRAS.405.1253K|doi = 10.1111/j.1365-2966.2010.16528.x |arxiv = 1002.3469 |year=2010 |doi-access=free |s2cid=55055925 }}</ref> and [[Kuiper belt objects]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Planet Formation by Coagulation: A Focus on Uranus and Neptune |first1=P.|last1=Goldreich |last2=Lithwick|first2=Y. |last3=Sari|first3=R. |journal=Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics| volume=42|issue=1|pages=549–601|bibcode=2004ARA&A..42..549G|arxiv = astro-ph/0405215 |doi = 10.1146/annurev.astro.42.053102.134004 |year=2004|s2cid=5177936}}</ref> Kenyon and Ben Bromley have suggested that the [[dwarf planet]] [[90377 Sedna|Sedna]] in the [[outer Solar System]] might be an exosolar object captured during a close encounter with another planetary system when the Sun was only a few million years old.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Two Young Stars Scuffle|first=Matthew |last=Quandt |journal=Astronomy |date=December 2004|url=http://www.astronomy.com/en/News-Observing/News/2004/12/Two%20young%20stars%20scuffle.aspx}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Distant object could hold secrets to Earth's past|last=Gugliotta |first=Guy|newspaper=Washington Post| date=13 February 2005|
url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/articles/A21549-2005Feb13.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Sun Might Have Exchanged Hangers-On With Rival Star|last=Overbye |first=Dennis| date=2 December 2004|newspaper=New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/12/02/science/02solar.html?pagewanted=print&position=&_r=0}}</ref> This capture mechanism might also explain other unusual [dwarf planets] such as {{mp|2004|XR 190}}<ref>{{cite news |title=How to explain a mini-planet's odd orbit?|newspaper=Christian Science Monitor |first=Peter|last=Spotts |date=19 December 2005 |url=https://www.csmonitor.com/2005/1219/p02s02-stss.html}}</ref>
